newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Organisers seek handover party sites in cramped HK.
newsitem.headline: Organisers seek handover party sites in cramped HK.

text.p: With just 55 days to go until Hong Kong's return to China, event organisers say they are scouring the territory for space to host hundreds of handover parties, celebrations, shows and firework extravaganzas.

Space is at a premium in the territory of 6.4 million people which is gearing up for the changes when the British furl their flag and depart at midnight on June 30 and Hong Kong once again becomes part of China.

The government has refused permission for a fireworks display off the south side of Hong Kong island, citing a lack of space for spectactors and concerns over crowd control, the South China Morning Post said on Wednesday.
Similar pyrotechnic displays on offshore islands have also been cancelled.

But two huge fireworks shows are planned over Hong Kong's famous harbour, one in the hours before the handover and another on July 1 as night falls and Hong Kong's first full day under the Chinese flag draws to a close.

Alongside the formal celebrations and festivities organised by the British and Chinese governments, hundreds of neighbourhood groups, bars, restaurants and hotels are gearing up for their own handover festivities.
Special menus and handover cocktails have been concocted. Souvenir T-shirts, mugs, toys and badges are flooding Hong Kong.
A 12-hour "rave" or dance party is being advertised on posters pasted up under cover of darkness in Hong Kong's entertainment district.

A group of revellers, well-known for their annual China coast ball, plan this year to party in Beijing and Shanghai before landing in Hong Kong for a grand finale at a cost of HK$16,380 ($2,000) per head, said one party-goer who plans to fly in from New York for the event.

The community-based Association for the Celebration of Reunification of Hong Kong with China said it was coordinating more than 100 events, including parades, street parties, folk music concerts and wanted a meeting with incoming leader Tung Chee-hwa to coordinate timetables.
Buddhist monks plan to release hundreds of pigeons to symbolise freedom.
A list is being drawn up of local pop stars and entertainers willing to perform free at events in the run-up to and beyond the handover.
